newsitem.title: FRANCE: AGF sees few Holocaust insurance claims.
newsitem.headline: AGF sees few Holocaust insurance claims.

text.p: French insurer AGF (Centrale des Assurances Generales de France) said on Tuesday it expected few claims from a U.S. lawsuit alleging that it and other European firms cheated Holocaust victims out of billions of dollars during the Nazi era.
"So far we haven't had any claims, though I'm not saying we won't be getting any," a spokesman for Assurances Generales de France said.
"If there is something, we will look into it, and of course, we will indemnify the people in the best way we can," the spokesman added.
The suit follows a campaign by Jewish groups to convince Swiss banks and several nations to return Nazi gold seized from Jews and other Holocaust victims during the World War Two era.

The insurance lawsuit, filed in late March in New York alleges that AGF and six other European insurers encouraged European citizens who feared persecution by the Nazis to deposit their assets with them and to purchase insurance to safeguard their families' futures.

The suit, initially filed on behalf of a small number of Holocaust victims and their families, alleges that the insurers withheld, concealed or converted the cash value and proceeds of policies sold before 1946, worth billions of dollars.

Lawyers filing the class-action complaint estimate that more than 10,000 people will eventually qualify to join the lawsuit as plaintiffs. The exact amount of damages, if any, would be determined at trial.

AGF officials said that according to court documents, just one individual, a woman from Brooklyn, had so far alleged as part of the suit that a relative had bought a policy from a corporate predecessor of AGF, which was not formed until two decades after the war.
Neither the woman nor her attorney had yet attempted to contact AGF directly to verify her claim or obtain additional information, the company spokesman said.
"We haven't heard anything at all from the lady," he said.
Others targeted in the suit in addition to AGF included Germany's largest insurer Allianz, fellow German insurer Bavarian Reinsurance and Italian companies Generali and RAS.
The firms have cited problems with tracing records which were lost or destroyed in the war and its immediate aftermath, when Europe was divided into East and West.
All of AGF's records from the war era were destroyed years ago and the firm would need independent evidence of a policy before it could do anything, company officials said.
